title: Our genie problem
content:
The djinn go back millennia, powerful and elusive creatures of the supernatural. They show up across time and culture.

Three hundred years ago, Charles Perrault retold a short story about a headstrong woodcutter and his wife. On being granted three wishes from Jupiter (archetype for the genie of legend), he accidentally blurts out that he’d like sausage for dinner. One wish, gone. His wife calls him a fool, and he responds by turning her nose into a sausage. Now, with just one wish left, he’s torn between being rich (but having a wife with a sausage attached to her nose) or using the third wish to end up right where he started.

Marital harmony and common sense prevail, and he ends up where he started, but filled with regret for what could have been. Ever since, we’ve been telling stories about people who screw up their wishes.

The persistence of genie morality in our culture is bigger than a Disney marketing ploy. It’s an important reminder about responsibility, long-term thinking and how often we fail to recognize how much agency we actually have. The three are woven into a narrative that often leaves us with a sausage attached to our noses.

In this moment, the biggest technology revolution humans have ever lived through, we’re all at risk of getting our wishes wrong. Careful what you wish for. But don’t forget to wish.

title: A Distant Star is Slowly Snacking on a Brown Dwarf
content:
Planets and stars usually have one of two kinds of relationship: Either a planet orbits its star in a fixed and stable circuit, or it flies too close to the sun (literally) and gets consumed by stellar wind and fire.

But now, for the first time, astronomers [have directly observed](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02992-6) an in-between state, a red dwarf star that’s absorbing material from a nearby brown dwarf, but very, very slowly. The transfer of material (or “accretion”) is happening at such a leisurely rate, it might be billions of years before the brown dwarf disappears altogether.

**Read more: “**[**This Spectacular Star Field Hides Brown Dwarfs That Never Ignite**](https://nautil.us/this-spectacular-star-field-hides-brown-dwarfs-that-never-ignite-1285482)**”**

Brown dwarfs are themselves in between two states. They’re larger than planets and smaller than stars, and are thus often considered “failed” stars that began to form but never properly ignited. This particular one is within the Milky Way, around 300 light-years from Earth, in a system that’s been named ZTF J0440+2325.

The star itself is relatively small, around 85 times the mass of Jupiter, while the brown dwarf is around 25 times the mass of Jupiter. The latter is orbiting the former every 87 minutes, which gives you an idea of how close they are.

The star (M. dwarf) and brown dwarf positions, with the path of the absorbed matter shown as the red line. _Credit: Householder et al., Nature Astronomy, 2026_

“When we think of stars interacting with planets or brown dwarfs, the picture is always that the star eventually swallows the other thing,” study author Kevin Burdge of MIT explained in a [statement](https://news.mit.edu/2026/astronomers-catch-star-slowly-snacking-on-brown-dwarf-1005). “This is what will happen to the Earth when the sun becomes a red giant. But here, we’ve found an alternative: Instead of swallowing the thing up, the star can gradually eat it, for billions of years.”

The first sign of this system came in a puzzling reading captured by experts: a triangular light signal that wouldn’t normally be given off by a star. It turns out the peak of that triangle was the fireball created by the star sucking in the brown dwarf, as it rotated in and out of view of a telescope at the Palomar Observatory in California.

It took several years to figure what was happening. The astronomers say the brown dwarf is dumping the equivalent of about 40 million dump trucks’ worth of material into its star every single second. That’s a lot, but also, we’re talking about an object with 85 times the mass of Jupiter.

Now that we know what one of these slow-feeding systems looks like, the hope is that more can be discovered. And with potentially billions of years of snacking time involved, we should have plenty of time to find them. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Babies Learn From Spit-Swapping
content:
Human babies are famously born completely helpless. Unable to even hold their heads up on their own, they rely on nearby humans for food, water, and the rest of their needs. That makes figuring out who can be counted on to provide those things pretty important for the little guys. According to a new study [published](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S109051382600139X) in the journal _Evolution and Human Behavior_, they might accomplish this important goal by watching who swaps spit.

“We were inspired by studies that found that across cultures, people in close relationships are often more comfortable sharing saliva with each other,” study author Brandon Woo of the University of California, Santa Barbara explained in a [statement](https://news.ucsb.edu/2026/022855/young-infants-infer-closeness-social-relationships-saliva-sharing-interactions). “So imagine seeing two people licking the same ice cream cone—could you guess how they might know each other?”

I could, but could a 4- to 6-month-old baby?

To find out, Woo and fellow psychologists from Harvard and MIT got their hands on some infants and treated them to a series of experimental puppet shows. In the first, an adult placed an orange slice in their mouth and then in the mouth of a puppet—a clear representation of saliva sharing. The team then had another adult pass a ball to the puppet to represent sharing without the spit.

**Read more:**[**“Do Babies Feel Shame?”**](https://nautil.us/do-babies-feel-shame-1285554)

In the next act of the production, the puppet expressed distress. The researchers monitored the infants to see which person (orange-sharer or ball-passer) they looked to as a signifier of which relationship they deemed closer, which is common in other primates. In studies of vervet monkeys, for example, juveniles will look to the mother of another juvenile if it emits a distress call.

The cast of the next puppet show included two puppet actors and a single human. It was also food-free. Instead of oranges, a human put their finger in their mouth, placed it in one puppet’s mouth, and then back in their own. They subsequently touched their forehead, touched the second puppet’s forehead, and then their own. After that bit of character development, the human protagonist acted like they were crying while the researchers watched which puppet the babies looked to.

“The first experiment focuses on a very familiar action: food sharing,” Woo explained. “The second behavior, with the finger in someone’s mouth versus someone else’s mouth, is not as common in children’s everyday lives.” (Hey, let’s hope so.)

The team found that in both scenarios, infants favored the saliva-sharers over the ball-passers or the forehead-touchers. Put simply, it seems the little tots inferred a certain closeness in the relationship of those who swapped spit.

It’s not the first time researchers have discovered babies making this inference, but it’s the first time in infants this young. The team performed the same experiment on babies between the ages of 8 and 10 months as part of another [study](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abh1054). By that age, 90 percent of babies are being fed solid food and are probably more familiar with witnessing the intimate behavior of saliva sharing, which means it may be learned. But between the age of 4 and 6 months, only around half of babies have started eating solid food.

In other words, these findings suggest representations of close social relationships could be part of a baby’s core knowledge, or the factory-installed firmware they’re born with. “It’s really cool that babies are still making inferences in both cases. That even with less familiar actions they’re making inferences about closeness,” Woo said. “It’s fascinating that they seem to have this abstract knowledge about relationships that applies across different actions.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Meet the New Otterlike Predator That Scurried Alongside Dinosaurs
content:
If the operators of _Jurassic Park_ were going for verisimilitude, they wouldn’t have just included flashy dinosaurs. There were plenty of tiny protomammals scurrying around at the time, as well. Now, paleontologists have unearthed a new kind of mammaliaform—and it’s a (relatively) big one.

An international team of paleontologists discovered the specimen in the collections of the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning in Shenyang, China, but it originated from a fossil assemblage in Mongolia. After a thorough analysis they [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11107-0) their findings in _Nature_, naming the mammaliaform _Megacauda sungei_.

**Read more: “[How Did Birds Outlive the Other Dinosaurs?](https://nautil.us/how-did-birds-outlive-the-other-dinosaurs-1284920)”**

The genus name is a reference to the critter’s flat, stout tail, which along with its short-haired coat and feet built for paddling, led the team to conclude it lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle. _M. sungei’s_ sharp, curved teeth would have been adept at capturing slippery prey, and at its size, it likely had its pick of food items. _M. sungei_ dwarfed other mammaliaforms living at the time (many of which resembled tiny shrews). It weighed in at over four pounds and was around a foot-and-a-half from snout to tail.

But according to the team, its real innovation was a little more inconspicuous. An analysis of the animal’s throat bones showed it likely had a soft palate separating its mouth from its pharynx that would have let it eat and drink while still breathing.

Crucially, in true mammals like us, the soft palate is also what allows us to suckle milk. “It was this adaptation that made brain development, eventually leading to humans, possible,” study author Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn explained in a [statement](https://www.uni-bonn.de/en/news/205-2026). “The soft palate and the shaping of the oral cavity and pharynx are directly linked to the evolution of mammals.”

It might not look like much, but this 18-inch swamp rat is family. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Forgive and Forget is Bad Advice
content:
Forgiveness is a core virtue across religious traditions the world over, but the concept seems to present a paradox. Forgetting past hurts can feel potentially catastrophic, making us vulnerable to similar offenses in the future from the original perpetrator or from others like them. But letting go may bring us peace from feelings of resentment, anger or hate. The memories of these hurts can haunt people for a lifetime, often leading to repeated violence or perpetual war, some of the worst scourges of humankind.

Duke University memory researcher, philosopher and cognitive scientist Felipe de Brigard has been studying the relationship between [memory and forgiveness](https://www.memoryandforgiveness.org/) since the early 2000s with a grant from the John Templeton Foundation. He has just won a MacArthur Foundation [grant](https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-2026/felipe-de-brigard) to continue pursuing that work.

**Read more:**[**“Are Some People Addicted to Revenge?”**](https://nautil.us/are-some-people-addicted-to-revenge-1238041)

De Brigard has specifically looked at how forgiveness and memory intersect for people living in a mountainous region near the northern coast of Colombia called Montes de María. Thousands of murders took place in this region from the 1980s through 2000, primarily at the hands of right-wing paramilitary forces. But because of how Colombia’s transitional justice and reconciliation process has proceeded, many of the paramilitary soldiers who demobilized and confessed their crimes are now living back in the same towns and rural districts with their former victims.

I spoke with De Brigard about what forgiveness does to the emotional weight of a painful memory, what his research tells us about how memory works, and what makes some offenses unforgivable.

**People are often told to “forgive and forget,” but your research into how forgiveness affects memory suggests this is bad advice. Why?**

Forgetting is a tricky term. It’s unclear exactly what people mean by that. The memory and forgiveness project is an offshoot of another project that I had been working on for almost a decade, which capitalizes on the fact that every time you remember a personal event, you risk changing the memory itself.

Most of the research on this process looks at the negative consequences. Typical examples are that the person sees someone mug someone else and then the cop comes and gives them some misinformation at the time of recollection, saying, “Oh, did you notice if the person was African American?” or something like that. Then that information, along with the biases of the individual, taint the content of the original memory such that when they remember it, it comes up as if the perpetrator was an African American.

I wanted to know, are there any positive consequences of the interaction between memory and imagination? And one of the positive consequences that we have explored is what is known as “emotional reappraisal.” Sometimes you have really negative memories, and one of these memories gets reactivated and then you do something in your mind to modify the emotion that is associated with that memory such that it doesn't hurt as much.

The particular kind of emotional reappraisal strategy that we had been exploring for those 10 years is what we call “downward counterfactual thinking.” Counterfactuals are imaginations about alternative ways in which past events could have occurred. A typical counterfactual that we engage in when we remember negative events is how things could be better, but that tends to generate a feeling of regret. The strategy that we employ is instead asking people to think about how a bad event could have been actually worse. And that generates a feeling of relief. “Well, at least I didn't die. At least I didn't lose my limbs,” or something like that.

That relief is a positive feeling that can be incorporated into the original memory so that the next time they remember it, it doesn’t hurt as much. That brings us to forgiveness. I started to think about other kinds of cognitive processes that could engage emotional reappraisal strategies. And I thought that forgiveness was one of them.

When you forgive, it’s not that you forget the event, but rather, now that you bring the event back to mind, now that you think about the perpetrator, now that you think about what happened, it doesn't elicit the same kind of negative affective reactions that it once did. The suggestion is, because we have emotionally reappraised the memory, we can bring ourselves to forgive. You don’t need to forget the contents of the memory. You just need to change the effect that is associated with the remembering.

**Obviously, for some minor offenses, it’s probably not terribly difficult, but for bigger ones, more extreme ones, especially if it’s at the level of violence against an entire community, or a genocide, something really extreme, I imagine this kind of emotional reappraisal can become much more difficult.**

Yes, for sure. That’s what is really fascinating. Most of my work is conducted both in Colombia and in the U.S. And in Colombia, where I'm from, I did research in Montes de María, which is in the northern part of Colombia, in an area that was terribly affected by violence for 40 years or so. In particular, in the early 2000s, that was just a really horrible period. We interview people from Montes de Maríaand take biophysiological measures from them. The data is in our favor, but what we have been trying to determine was whether forgiveness led to a change in affect associated with painful memories in both the US and Colombia.

We have seen it in the US, as you say, with relatively easy offenses, such as if someone said something mean to a person on Facebook. But as you say, severity seems to be an important factor here. And we have observed it in the United States, but I wanted to see it in Colombia as well. And you actually do. It’s remarkable. You see a reduction in the affective reaction, in the intensity with which the memory is remembered.

And not only verbal self-reports, we also measure objective physiological response. We measure facial expressions, heart rate, respiration, skin conductance, all those things that are associated with the expression of emotions. And you actually see it there, too. Another paper that we just published recently also suggests that the reduction in affect occurs regardless of the severity of the offense, and it also occurs regardless of how close the perpetrator was to you. We seem to have identified something that is essential to the experience of forgiveness.

**How does someone actually get to forgiveness in these scenarios? Can you describe the mental process of letting go of that hurt and anger?**

I wish there were a single technique. First of all, the person needs to want to forgive. And there are lots of reasons why someone might want to forgive. In the context of the post-conflict areas where I work in Colombia, there’s a very strong motivator to want to forgive, which is the fact that the perpetrators are back to living in the same community with you.

This is not like a situation in which I hated my roommate who did something terrible to me, so I decided to move to another house. You don’t have that possibility. There are plenty of people who live in conflict-torn zones that don’t have the possibility, the means, to move to a different place. And in Colombia, because it was a war, and because of the transitional justice process, it’s not like the perpetrators are going to go to prison. They are reincorporated into society. You find these communities where former guerrilla members and former paramilitaries that attacked communities are now back to living in the same areas. For this reason, forgiveness is an extremely desirable process to go through because it helps you to live with your past without it hurting as much. But willingness to forgive is extremely important, too, and not everyone is willing to forgive.

But what do you think is the most predictive factor determining whether you’re going to forgive or not? It’s an apology. If the perpetrator apologizes, more than if the perpetrator atones, your likelihood of forgiving just increased. There are a number of other factors that can pile on to increase the likelihood of forgiveness: empathizing with the perpetrator, seeing things from their perspective, thinking about the positive consequences that a bad action could have brought to your life. All of these things are a part of this emotional reappraisal strategy that I was telling you about and all of them can be combined. It’s not like a recipe, though, in the sense that if you follow all the steps you’re guaranteed to forgive, but they increase your chances.

But one of the things that we are very clear with the community about is that forgiveness is absolutely not mandatory. There are unforgivable offenses, and I don’t think that forgiving is morally obligatory. But one of the great advantages of the approach that we take is that we are separating the process of forgiveness from the underlying mechanism of emotional reappraisal. We believe that forgiveness involves this emotional reappraisal that I was telling you about, but it’s not the only emotional reappraisal strategy. There are other emotional reappraisal strategies that can help you to bring about that desired emotional change. So even for folks who cannot bring themselves to forgive, who don’t want to forgive, but do want the emotional change, offering the possibility that other techniques, borrowed from cognitive behavioral therapy and so forth, are available, provides a little bit of a relief. A sense of forgiveness is not the only mechanism for reconciliation.

**Are there unforgivable offences? What kinds of offenses are these?**

Forgivability is what we philosophers call a moral term. It’s a term that talks about possibilities. Things can be unforgivable or hard to forgive for various reasons. In the context of war, for instance, many times the perpetrator just doesn’t exist because the perpetrator was killed in the conflict, and there is no one who can apologize for a massacre. It’s tricky to forgive someone if you don’t even know who that person might be. It’s difficult to forgive someone who passed away. If they were still alive, would they feel bad?

Imagine, even worse, forgiving someone you don't know, a soldier or a guerrilla member who killed your mom in the conflict zone, and then was, in turn, killed in another battle, and no one knows who that person was, no one knows the circumstances. There was a perpetrator that did the most horrible thing that could have happened to you, and you’re in a peace process in which you’re asked to forgive the perpetrator, which is a member of a large group, say FARC [the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia]. That’s a very tricky one, right?

That’s one kind of unforgivability, because there is no one to forgive. But there is another kind of unforgivability. When is it morally incorrect or morally wrong to forgive someone? That is a philosophically complex questio,n and views vary. Some folks in philosophy think that forgiveness is mandatory, that when you are asked for forgiveness, it is your responsibility, it’s your duty actually to forgive the perpetrator. Theistic views sometimes posit this.

I don’t subscribe to this view, and the argument for me is that it seems strange when you’ve been wronged to acquire a duty to do something good for someone else. I don’t love thinking about forgiveness in this way. It might be possible that forgiving someone would actually break an even more important principle. One thing that seems very clear is that if you’re unbelievably forgiving, if you forgive anything, even offenses that you think are completely contrary to your dignity, maybe forgiving breaks another moral norm.

**I would imagine also in certain circumstances, it could make you more vulnerable to continued or future abuse.**

Absolutely. I had a former graduate student of mine, who’s now a professor in business school in Singapore, who was also interested in forgiveness. And one of the things that he discovered in his work is that if you are in the corporate world, and you’re very forgiving, it could work against you. Suppose that your boss constantly asks you to work extra hours. Being extremely forgiving is like, “Yeah, sure, I’ll do it. No worries.” And then, they apologize. Then it leaves you more vulnerable for exploitation. Too much forgiveness seems to be bad. Too little forgiveness also seems to be bad. You don’t want to work with someone who’s completely unforgiving. Like, “Oh, I accidentally used your mug,” and the person goes, “Well, that’s it!” Some sweet spot in the middle seems to be ideal.

**You mentioned that if a person does not want to forgive, there are other ways to blunt the pain of a memory or experience. What are those alternatives?**

Within cognitive behavioral therapy, people have employed different strategies for emotional reappraisal. The most well-known are things like temporal distancing. Suppose that something bad happens to you, and it’s like, “Oh, this is the worst thing. I’m never gonna survive that.” But then you imagine how you will feel 10 years from now about this thing. When I was in college, I remember I broke up with my girlfriend, and I thought, “This is the end of my life. It’s just terrible.” And one of the strategies was to think, “Well, you’re 20. Think how you’re going to feel about this ten years from now. It’s gonna be okay.” That projection into the future helps to assuage or mollify the negativity.

Another option is remembering painful events in a context that makes them more positive, that positive affect sort of contaminates the original memory and then it just doesn’t hurt as much next time you remember. So that’s one downward counterfactual that I was mentioning, that’s the one we have. Which ones are more conducive to forgiveness? We don’t know. That is actually the second part of the memory and forgiveness project that we are working on now. I was looking for support to continue with this project, so this MacArthur award is going to go mostly to that.

**What other kinds of techniques of reappraisal are you exploring that might be helpful for forgiveness?**

There are a few others. We have six in the proposal that we’re going to be studying. So emotional distancing is one. There’s another one called “meaning making.” There’s counterfactual thinking. There is empathy. Empathy plays a super important role. Like if you empathize with the person, see them as a human.

The problem with empathy in post-conflict zones is that it’s easier to empathize when you have a concrete individual you can think of, right? It’s tough to empathize with an abstract individual, like when you don't know who the perpetrator is. We’re going to be testing several ones, but I don’t know if all of them are going to be equally applicable for all the scenarios that we’ll be facing because we face lots of different kinds of criminal and war horrors.

Right now, I’m working in Montes de María, but there are a bunch of other teams in Colombia that are interested in doing something similar, so we might expand it to three or four more territories. And now I’m in conversations with other groups in other areas of the world where we’re hoping to be able to evaluate forgiveness, too, and to try for strategies of cognitive reappraisal or emotional reappraisal to see if it helps over there as well.

**Your work has looked at competing theories about how forgiveness affects memory in the brain. You looked at “emotional fading”****versus “episodic fading.” And I was really surprised to learn that you found forgiveness only works on emotional fading, not episodic fading. In other words, it reduces the emotional weight of the memory, but it doesn’t reduce how detailed or vivid the memory is. Does that tell us anything more global about the way memory works?**

Yes. It tells you one thing that is very clear and something that I have become more and more convinced of throughout my career: Memory is not a monolithic phenomena. It’s not like you have one memory, and the memory either dies or is preserved as a whole. In fact, something that is super cool is that different details of the memory are forgotten at different rates.

And memories are also a composite of information about space, about people, about objects, about feelings, about intensities of those feelings, about light. Like all those things are composite. It turns out that they’re relatively easy to differentiate in your mental representation if you want.

An example that I give to people is that when you stop talking to someone for a long time—this occurs with dead loved ones—if you try to picture their faces, you can sometimes do that easily. But it’s hard to imagine their voices, right? Obviously, we now have recordings that can trigger the memory of an absent person’s voice. But without this recording, it is very difficult to remember a voice. You might remember mannerisms, faces, but not voices. Why? Because the contents of those memories are not lost all the same at the same rate. They’re not all preserved equally.

**That’s wild. Do we understand why voice is harder to remember?**

There might be some individual variability there, too. Some people might remember voices better than others, but, no, I don’t know exactly why. We’re a very visual and spatial species. We preserve memories of spaces extraordinarily well, better than objects, sounds, or tastes.

One possible explanation is that evolutionarily, we were foragers, and we really needed to remember where we left the food that we caught, where we saw the saber-toothed tiger that wanted to attack us and so forth. If you think about it, you probably can remember spaces from your childhood extremely well, but you’re going to have a harder time remembering the faces of people you knew in elementary school. There is a kind of hierarchy of preservation of different kinds of contents in memory.

**Does self-forgiveness generally affect memory in the same way that these other forms of forgiveness do?**

In fact, one of my current students is working on self-forgiveness. It is tricky though, because you are both the perpetrator and the victim. It is up to you to ask for forgiveness, but it is also up to you to forgive. My student who has been working on self-forgiveness has been looking at what kinds of wrongs we tend to blame ourselves for and forgive ourselves for. She’s looking into whether similar emotional reappraisal mechanisms that we have seen with interpersonal forgiveness also work with self-forgiveness, so the jury is still out, but we’re working on that.

**How has your view of the nature of forgiveness changed over the course of the memory and forgiveness project?**

When I first started thinking about forgiveness six years or so ago, I thought that forgiveness was a dyadic relationship. That is to say between a perpetrator and a victim. Typically when you lead work on forgiveness, the idea is that forgiveness is there to repair a relationship. Most of the empirical research or psychological research on forgiveness is with couples therapies. One cheats on the other, or treats the other poorly, and then they really want to repair the relationship. Forgiveness is employed as a way of repairing the relationship.

But there is an enormous amount of variability on when forgiveness is called for, and there are lots of different variations depending on the relationship you have to the person you’re forgiving: Forgiving your partner is different than forgiving your boss is different than forgiving the person sitting next to you on the bus.

Sometimes forgiveness is the way in which you can split from another person without hurt. Sometimes forgiveness as it happens in the context of war occurs between two people who have never met each other and that have no plans whatsoever to have a relationship afterwards.

And sometimes, even more strangely, especially in the context of war, forgiveness occurs not between a victim and a direct perpetrator—because both might be dead—but rather between a representative of the group to which the perpetrator belonged and a representative of the group to which the victim belonged.

And finally, there is also an argument to be made that even with all this weirdness of different relationships, that sometimes it’s not dyadic, that sometimes it’s not between two parties. Sometimes it’s between three parties. The two coinvestigators I work with in Colombia think that forgiveness in many of these communities is actually a tripartite relationship that involves a perpetrator, a victim, and a community.

The kind of relationship involved in different practices of forgiveness is really important. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How to Live to Be 194 Years Old
content:
In 1882, four Aldabra giant tortoises were captured by British officials in the Seychelles and loaded onto a ship, which then traveled nearly 3,000 nautical miles to the British colony of St. Helena. The tortoises (_Aldabrachelys gigantea_) were gifted to Sir William Grey-Wilson, the governor of St. Helena Island, to live on the grounds of his home.

While Grey-Wilson [died a century ago](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/281146905/william-grey-wilson), one of the tortoises, “Jonathan,” is still alive. Based on Jonathan’s size when he arrived in St. Helena, he was already 50 years old, making him now 194 years old. And Jonathan is a gift that keeps on giving.

**Read more:**[**“The Tortoises That Inspired Modern Robotics”**](https://nautil.us/the-tortoises-that-inspired-modern-robotics-1268922)

A [new study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adw8887) of his genes and associated chemical switches (the epigenome) has illuminated how giant tortoises achieve such unparalleled longevity. Led by U.S. geneticists and published today in _Science Advances_, the study put forth a model for tortoise age-resistance that entails a positive feedback loop between DNA repair, ATP production, and other key cellular activities.

“Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan’s genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience,” explained senior author Stephen Clark, founder of longevity nonprofit [Kallel Foundation](https://www.kallel.org/).

The research team sequenced Jonathan’s genome from cheek swags and saliva and assayed his methylome, a signature that shows how the genome has been epigenetically modified by the environment. They found a whopping 287 unique gene variants that limit the effects of aging by repairing DNA, stemming inflammation, regulating insulin, and suppressing cancer.

They also found that the epigenetic switches turning the genes on and off were akin to those of younger Aldabra tortoises. In humans, our epigenome changes over time, leading to degradation of our bodies as anti-aging genes shut off. In contrast, Jonathan still has all his anti-aging tools at work in his nearly 200-year-old body.

“Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject,” remarked study author Justin Gerlach from the University of Cambridge in a [press release](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1146346).

Jonathan might look old, but don’t let that fool you—he still has plenty of spring in his step and, most importantly, vigor in his cells. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Neanderthals Were Adept Woodworkers Too
content:
The traditional Neanderthal stereotype might be that of a club-wielding caveman, but they actually had some pretty sophisticated technology. Our archaic cousins fashioned all manner of delicate instruments out of flakes of flint and other stone, including scrapers, axes, knives—even [dentist drills](https://nautil.us/how-neanderthals-mastered-dentistry-1280722). Of course, that’s not the extent of the Neanderthal toolkit, only what survived to be scrutinized by us tens of thousands of years later. Most Neanderthal wooden tools have unfortunately been lost to the ravages of time—with a few exceptions.

Abric Romaní, a cliffside settlement in Spain occupied by Neanderthals around 70,000 to 39,000 years ago, contains evidence of wooden objects preserved by travertine incrustation. During this process, calcium carbonate builds up around the wood, which decays, leaving an impression so detailed it’s possible to make out individual plant cells. A new study of this rare assemblage [published](http://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aeh2287?adobe_mc=MCMID%3D67574973318743701110145551447064163025%7CMCORGID%3D242B6472541199F70A4C98A6%2540AdobeOrg%7CTS%3D1791320420) in _Science Advances_ offers insight into the lives of our distant relatives.

****Read more:**[**“How Neanderthals Mastered Dentistry”**](https://nautil.us/how-neanderthals-mastered-dentistry-1280722)**

Researchers from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution peeled back 16 archeological levels documenting roughly 20,000 years of Neanderthal occupation (from around 62,000 to 40,000 years ago). They meticulously documented the impressions left by almost 600 wooden objects buried there during that time.

“Though relatively small, this collection of artifacts is notable for the varied morphology and functionality of the items that comprise it, demonstrating a remarkable technological versatility and the diversified exploitation of wood as a raw material,” the researchers wrote.

The team found domestic objects such as a series of trays made from bark, some with concave depressions like plates. They also discovered a cache of Scots pine firewood piled against a rear wall (Neanderthals seem to like to keep a tidy living area, too). A tripod structure consisting of three wooden poles could have been a frame for a windbreak to protect an entrance from the elements, according to the team. They found a series of pointed sticks as well, some of which seemed to be spears while others may have functioned as digging implements used to find tubers and other underground food sources.

The impression of a Neanderthal “club” preserved in rock at the Abric Romaní site. _Credit: M.D. Guillén/IPHES_

Their most remarkable find was a wooden club, which the team called “the most exceptional wooden object identified in the assemblage to date.” Around a foot long, the tool showed signs of deliberate scraping and shaping. It had a distinct handle with a slightly flared base to prevent it from slipping out of the hand. The business end extended 90 degrees from the handle and curved slightly, leading the researchers to surmise it was used for striking (although they couldn’t rule out other uses, like digging).

What, exactly, these Neanderthals were striking remains a mystery but the researchers noted that similar clubs are used by hunter-gatherer tribes for “interpersonal violence, hunting, and fishing.” So it might be true that Neanderthals were club-wielding cavemen after all, but they were also talented woodworkers. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Most Curious Cloud on Mars Relies on Some Bizarre Physics
content:
If you ever get a chance to stand at the foot of the giant Arsia Mons volcano on Mars during spring or summer dusty season, you’ll witness one of the solar system’s most spectacular sights around dawn: the dramatic appearance of the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC).

First, a cloud forms overhead, caused by air getting pushed up the sides of the volcano, where scant amounts of water vapor in the atmosphere freezes. Then, it forms a trail that pushes out across the expanse of the sky, driven by winds up to 373 miles per hour.

**Read more: “**[**The New Seismic Discovery Beneath the Surface of Mars**](https://nautil.us/the-new-seismic-discovery-beneath-the-surface-of-mars-1282289)**”**

The scales are vast. Arsia Mons is more than twice the height of Mount Everest, and the ice cloud stretches almost 1,120 miles—or about one-and-a-half times the length of California. Then, in a few hours, as the sun rises and the air warms, it’s gone, only to reappear again like clockwork the next morning.

An icy trail extends for nearly 1,120 miles. _Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin/J. Cowart_

Of course, we can’t observe the AMEC from the ground yet, but the Mars Express probe has been watching it closely from orbit since 2018, and researchers have now discovered that this incredible meteorological phenomenon involves some pretty unusual physics.

A new [study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02089-9) has managed to find a simulation model that fits the AMEC, and it removes an element that’s typically essential for formation of these types of clouds. Such [orographic clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orographic_lift) are found on Earth too, but they usually require some kind of particles for the ice to cling on to—salt, pollen, soot, or dust, for example.

With the AMEC, it was thought that dust was acting as an ice crystal carrier. The latest hypothesis, however, is that the ice forms all by itself. “For the AMEC, it seems that cloud formation takes place without needing any of this ‘stuff,’” study author Jorge Hernández-Bernal explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1146107). “Water vapor turns directly into icy cloud particles without any middle step. It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window.”

The AMEC in context with the rest of the Red Planet. _Credit: ESA/GCP/UPV/EHU Bilbao_

Technically it’s known as homogeneous nucleation, and it’s the first time it’s been seen in a planetary atmosphere, with the researchers describing it as “wholly unexpected.” Physics can explain it, but only via an exotic level previously theorized rather than observed, and reliant on very rare circumstances.

To that end, the researchers think the height of Arsia Mons, the thinness of the atmosphere, and the extreme relative humidity—potentially more than 100,000 times more than what is typical on Earth—all combine to produce the required very rare circumstances.

That said, while the new model is the best one yet for AMEC, there are still unexplained discrepancies. It’s a reminder that other planets have events that are genuinely out of this world. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Top Forecasters On The Plague
content:
A technician at a Siberian lab has [died of yersinia infection aka plague](https://apnews.com/article/russia-plague-trump-who-irkutsk-5aa82b8bc3d8300c551cd0e1bf91e32c). The details are fuzzy, but the lab seems to have been working with pneumonic plague, an especially contagious and dangerous form. A few articles quote authorities as saying the risk is small.

What about forecasters?

[Sentinel Global Risks Watch](https://blog.sentinel-team.org/about)[1](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/top-forecasters-on-the-plague#footnote-1) are the people best placed to have an opinion on this. They are a team of tournament-winning superforecasters who provide probabilities on upcoming risks as a public service, and their track record is excellent. [They say](https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/open-model-reaches-mythos-hacking):

> Our forecasters think there’s a **0.7%** (0.1% to 2.0%) chance that there will be more than 1,000 deaths attributed to plague across the globe in the next 12 months. The low probability stems from the lack of known further cases, the initial rapid isolation of contacts, and the ability to contain the spread of typical plague outbreaks with antibiotics. However, we note the possibility that the worker may have died from infection with an antibiotic-resistant strain of plague or from a completely different disease that may or may not have been related to her work at the institute. While some commentators online are drumming up alarm, we mostly think this is unjustified at this time because there is currently no report of onward spread of any disease and strict quarantine measures have reportedly been implemented. Thus, we consider this a serious incident that merits monitoring _but not alarm_ at this time. It is also a good opportunity for readers to consider taking some general pandemic preparedness measures in their own homes, buy some PPE, perhaps some [far-UVC lights](https://aerolamp.net/)[2](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/top-forecasters-on-the-plague#footnote-2), think about what would be good rural places to go to and how, etc., not because of this incident in particular but taking it as a prompt.
> 
> 
> Some of our forecasters think that the real story is, to some extent, not whether there was a pneumonic plague death or whether there might be a small pneumonic plague outbreak, which [happen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st-century_Madagascar_plague_outbreaks) periodically around the world, but whether and the extent to which the Russian government might have been developing bioweapons in the worker’s institute, and [whether](https://x.com/ashishkjha/status/2106907902183166346) the current situation may have resulted from a bioweapons lab accident. This incident is also worrying because it confirms our estimation that the risks from lab leaks, and especially bioweapons lab leaks, are a latent worry.

What about [the AI superforecasters](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-superforecasters-are-here)? AIs [recently beat](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters) the top human forecasters in the Metaculus Cup for the first time, so the machines may now be even more trustworthy than Sentinel. I asked two.

[FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/)[said](https://futuresearch.ai/app/p/a/will-there-be-more-than-1-000-deaths-from):

> Probability: **1%**. The baseline rate of global plague mortality is far below the 1,000-death threshold, typically averaging around 60 deaths per year. According to the WHO’s 2019–2025 review, 10 countries reported 3,847 suspected cases and 423 deaths over the seven-year period . The highest single-year death toll during this time was 79 in 2023 . Crucially, these counts already incorporate suspected, probable, and confirmed cases across all clinical forms—bubonic, pneumonic, and septicaemic . Exceeding 1,000 deaths would require an event roughly 13 times deadlier than the worst recent year.
> 
> 
> The recent death of a lab worker at a Russian anti-plague institute in Irkutsk in early October 2026 raises vigilance, but current evidence suggests the incident is contained. Russian authorities deny a lab accident and report “pneumonia of unknown aetiology” . The WHO states that Russia has reported no confirmed plague cases and assesses the risk of broader spread as very low . Approximately 190 contacts have been identified, monitored, and tested with no dangerous pathogens detected or secondary symptomatic cases emerging . Because pneumonic plague develops rapidly, the lack of onward transmission weeks after the initial exposure strongly indicates this chain of infection is over, leaving the probability of an outbreak exceeding 1,000 deaths highly remote.

On further questioning, it said that even that 1% was mostly just that the regular epidemics in Madagascar got especially bad this year, and the chance of a global pandemic starting with the Russian lab was “effectively zero”.

And [Preseen](https://preseen.com/dashboard)[said](https://preseen.com/questions/ca5afbae-84c4-4100-a7c3-fc58f1d28357?forecast=6d9d1d56-e622-40a5-8b7b-ac74dbbf5dd3):

> **0.2% chance**. I assign less than 1% probability to a YES resolution. The Russian incident has not established secondary cases or sustained transmission ([ECDC assessment](https://www.ecdc.europa.eu/en/news-events/ecdc-closely-monitoring-situation-following-case-pneumonia-unknown-origin-russia)). YES requires both an exceptional mortality surge and qualifying WHO reporting that places enough deaths inside the specified window.

What about prediction markets? Polymarket [is currently at 5%](https://polymarket.com/event/plague-pandemic-in-2026) for WHO declaring plague a “pandemic”, but markets are notoriously bad at handling very small probabilities, so I don’t take it seriously as a counter to the sources above.

I think this is a good example of a situation where technical forecasting is helpful. I felt underserved by mainstream articles, which either tried to maintain journalistic neutrality by giving no opinion, or quoted scientists’ vague statements saying not to worry. Given that all three top forecaster sources were 1% or less, and the statement they were forecasting was much weaker than the scenario we’re worried about (eg it includes other sources of plague epidemics, it starts at 1000 deaths rather than a true global pandemic, etc), I think they’re sending a strong message that this isn’t a direct cause for concern (although I agree with Sentinel that this is a good indirect reminder that lab leaks, bioweapons, and pandemics all remain ever-present dangers).

[1](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/top-forecasters-on-the-plague#footnote-anchor-1)
